4 · One habit, five ways of reporting it.
I have a nap before every night shift.  →  a present habit.

I used to have a nap before every shift.  →  past, and no longer true.

1 · Read the explanation.
Present habits, past habits, and the two used tos

English has one straightforward way of describing a present habit and two competing ways of describing a past one. The present is the easy half: the present simple, usually with an adverb of frequency — I never sleep on planes, she usually has a nap after lunch. If you want to insist that it is true, add the auxiliary do: I really do need my sleep. And if a repeated action irritates you, English has a special form for that: always with the present continuous, as in they are always getting up before six.

Past habits. Used to + infinitive covers both actions and states that were true once and are not now: I used to sleep on planes, we used to live in Almaty, she used to be a light sleeper. Would + infinitive covers repeated past actions only, and it needs a time frame around it, which is why it belongs to storytelling rather than to a single statement: on night shifts I would have a nap, walk to the station and buy a coffee. You cannot say I would live in Almaty or I would be a light sleeper; states take used to.

The past simple is still available, and is better when the number of times is given or when the habit belongs to a defined period: she flew there twice a year for a decade.

Negatives and questions. The d disappears: I didn’t use to sleep well, Did you use to work nights? This is the most frequent written error with this structure.

The other used to. Be used to and get used to are followed by a noun or an -ing form and describe being, or becoming, accustomed to something: I am used to sleeping badly on flights, you will get used to the light. Nothing about them is past, and confusing them with used to do is the classic B2 error.

Frequency adverbs
  • Mid position, before the main verb: I never sleep on planes.
  • After be: She is always tired on Mondays.
  • Longer expressions go at the end: twice a week, every other day, most nights.
  • Hardly ever and rarely are already negative: I hardly ever have a lie-in, not don’t hardly ever.

Two things to watch

1 — Would cannot carry a state. I would have a car, I would live there and I would be tired are all wrong as past habits. If the verb is be, have (own), live, know, like or believe, use used to.

2 — No d after did. Didn’t used to is very common in speech and is treated as an error in writing. Write didn’t use to and did you use to.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Present habits, and the two ways of colouring them

The plain present simple states a routine, usually with a frequency adverb: She has a snooze after lunch most days · I never sleep a wink on a night flight. Two structures colour it. Emphatic do insists that the habit really is true, often against doubt: I really do need eight hours · I did try — earplugs, eye mask, everything. always + present continuous reports a repeated action the speaker finds annoying or surprising: He is always nodding off in meetings. Said with the present simple (He always nods off) it is a neutral fact; with the continuous it is a complaint.

Past habits: what used to and would can each do

used to + infinitive covers both past actions and past states that are no longer true: I used to fall asleep in front of the television · She used to be a very light sleeper. would + infinitive covers repeated past actions only: Every summer we would sleep outside on the balcony. It cannot carry a state, which is why I would be a light sleeper is wrong and I used to be is right. would also needs a past time frame already established; it cannot open a story cold.

Negatives and questions lose the d: I didn’t use to sleep well · Did you use to nap? And keep used to apart from be used to + -ing, which means accustomed: I am used to working nights — present, not past, and a completely different structure.

The past simple is still needed for one occasion, and for a habit whose number of times is given: I put in the earplugs · She flew there twice a year for ten years.

Errors to watch: I use to sleep badly (as a past habit) → used to · I didn’t used to → didn’t use to · I would be a light sleeper → used to be · I am used to work nights → used to working.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

How I sleep now, and how I used to

A sleep researcher is collecting accounts from ordinary people rather than from a laboratory.

The brief

The study wants three things from each person: what a normal week looks like now, what it looked like ten years ago, and the single occasion that changed it or proved it. The researchers are not interested in advice — only in what actually happens, and how often.

1 · Make notes before you speak. One line each.
1Your week now, with two frequency adverbs:
2What you used to do ten years ago:
3A repeated action from one period of your life:
4The occasion that changed it, or proved the rule:
5One thing you have become used to:
2 · Take the two roles, then swap.
Useful language

1 · Read the model.
Model · an account for the study

Most weeks now I am in bed by eleven and wide awake at half past five, usually before the alarm and always before anybody else in the flat. I hardly ever have a lie-in, even on Sunday, and I have stopped pretending that I want one. Twice a week I have a twenty-minute nap after work, which I really do need on the days I teach in the evening.

Ten years ago the pattern was almost the opposite. I used to go to bed at two and get up at nine, and I did not use to think of that as a problem. In my last year at university I would work until the middle of the night, sleep through the morning, and fall asleep again in the afternoon lectures — which is the only part of it I would still defend.

What changed it was one flight. It was thirteen hours, I did try everything, and I did not sleep a wink; I arrived exhausted, taught for three days in that state and decided the whole approach was a mistake. Nothing medical, nothing dramatic: I simply stopped enjoying being tired.

I am used to the early mornings now, and to the silence that comes with them, although for the first two months I was a light sleeper for the first time in my life and blamed the neighbours for it. These days I sleep like a log, and the only thing I still find difficult is a plane.
